raw.answer: Two groups of workers tried to register enterprise unions at their own workplaces (a maintenance plant and another aviation company site). Their registrations were repeatedly overturned because a regulation required a workplace to have independent personnel, budget and accounting. The Constitutional Court held that the regulation was made without clear authorization from the statute and so violates the legal reservation principle, though it is not disproportionate, and it sent both cases back to the Supreme Administrative Court.
raw.held: The two paragraphs of the Enforcement Rules of the Labor Union Act defining a 'workplace' (廠場) violate the constitutional legal reservation principle and lose effect at the latest two years after the judgment is announced; they do not violate the proportionality principle. The two Supreme Administrative Court judgments are overturned and sent back.

points.text: Forming unions is protected by the freedom of association, and rules on who may form a union must follow the legal reservation principle and the proportionality principle.
Defining the 'same workplace' decides whether workers can form a workplace enterprise union, so it is an important matter affecting their right of association.
The Labor Union Act does not define 'workplace' or clearly authorize the agency to set these requirements, so the regulation violates the legal reservation principle.
The regulation's aim is legitimate: preventing fragmented unions and ensuring workplaces have the management function to bargain on equal terms with employers.
The means have a reasonable link to that aim, since too many small unions could weaken bargaining power, so the regulation does not violate proportionality.
Because the judgments applied the unconstitutional regulation, they are overturned and returned so the courts can apply law free of that defect.

who: Workers seeking to form workplace unions
Existing enterprise unions
Employers
Labor authorities

raw.answer: Eight people had been convicted of criminal defamation for things they posted, sent or wrote about others. They asked Taiwan's Constitutional Court to review the defamation rules in the Criminal Code and, in two cases, the court judgments. The court held the rules are constitutional as long as they are applied with a reasonable-fact-checking safeguard, and it rejected all eight petitions.
raw.held: The defamation provisions (Criminal Code Articles 310 and 311) do not violate the Constitution, provided that a speaker on a public-interest matter who reasonably checked the facts beforehand, and who did not knowingly or recklessly rely on false evidence, is not punished. All eight petitions were dismissed as without merit.

points.text: Free speech and reputation are both constitutionally protected. When they conflict, the court must balance them, giving weight to how much the speech contributes to public debate.

Criminal punishment of defamation aims to protect the constitutional right to reputation. It is suitable for that goal, and no equally effective, less harmful alternative exists. The exceptions in Articles 310(3) and 311 further narrow the punishable range.

The exception for purely private-life matters unrelated to public interest is acceptable. Proving such matters true would intrude on the privacy of the person described, so speech there yields to reputation and privacy.
For public-interest matters, 'truth' does not require absolute objective truth. Requiring that would stifle news reporting, and speakers also owe a duty to verify facts.

A speaker who reasonably checked the facts beforehand and relied on false evidence without knowledge or serious recklessness is not punished. Prosecutors or private accusers must prove such bad intent. Without reasonable checking, or with bad intent, reputation takes priority.

How careful the checking must be depends on the case. Speech on media or social platforms needs more rigorous checking, while speech with high public-debate value gets more room for error if there is no bad intent.

who: People convicted of or facing defamation charges
People who post or publish factual claims about others, including on social media
News media and other publishers
People whose reputation is harmed by statements

raw.answer: Five people convicted in criminal cases challenged a Criminal Procedure Code rule. Under it, a police-interview statement from a witness who has died, or who cannot be found or brought to court, may be used as evidence. The Constitutional Court held the rule is not unconstitutional, provided courts apply it strictly and protect the defendant's right to defend himself or herself, and provided such a statement is never the only or main basis for a guilty verdict.
raw.held: The challenges by all five petitioners to Article 159-3, items 1 and 3, were rejected, because the rule is constitutional within the limits the court set. Petitioners 1 and 3's remaining requests were not accepted, and petitioners 4 and 5's requests for a temporary order were rejected.

points.text: Defendants have a constitutional right to a fair trial and full defense, including questioning witnesses in court. A witness's out-of-court statement, if the witness was never questioned in court, generally cannot be used to convict.

The legislature may make exceptions in the public interest of finding the truth, if the defendant gets fair compensation for the lost defense rights and the statement is not the only or main proof of guilt.

The rule's statutory conditions are strict: the witness must be dead or unfindable and cannot be brought to court. The statement must also be shown to have been made in specially trustworthy circumstances and be necessary to prove the facts. The prosecutor bears the burden of proof, and the defendant may contest these conditions.

Because the defendant cannot question such a witness, the court must make up for that loss. It can let the defendant question the interviewer and others when deciding whether the statement is admissible, and strengthen the defendant's questioning of witnesses who do appear.

The court may not use such a statement as the only or main evidence of guilt. Other solid supporting evidence is needed. Within these limits, the rule does not violate Articles 8 and 16 of the Constitution.

Some requests were not accepted because the other rules and the resolution challenged were not applied in the final judgments. The temporary-order requests were rejected because the main requests had been decided.

who: Criminal defendants
Witnesses who did not appear in court
Courts and judges
Prosecutors

raw.answer: A candidate who lost a 2022 township representative election in Hsinchu County by just 2 votes asked a court to recount the ballots, but was refused because the recount rule covers only some elections. The Constitutional Court found that the rule, by leaving out other public office elections, violates the constitutional guarantee of equality. It sent the candidate's case back to the High Court.
raw.held: The recount rule is unconstitutional to the extent it excludes elections other than district and indigenous legislators, special municipality mayors and county or city mayors. Until the law is fixed, the top losing candidate in any public office election, within 0.3% of the lowest winning vote count, may request a recount. The High Court's ruling is quashed and sent back, and the challenge to the second ruling is not accepted.

points.text: Rules on how elections are run or challenged must respect equal protection. Different treatment needs an important public-interest purpose and a substantial link between the classification and that purpose.
The recount rule aims to ensure accurate and fair results, protect the right to stand for office, and settle disputes quickly. These are important public interests shared by all democratic elections.
The rule treats elections differently by type, allowing recounts only in three kinds of elections and excluding all others.

The reasons given by the government, such as greater public attention and saving judicial resources, do not show a proper purpose. Every election matters equally, and saving resources is not an important constitutional interest.
Counting errors can happen in any election, so the classification works against the rule's own purpose of accurate results and has no substantial link to it.

Because the rule is unconstitutional, the High Court ruling based on it is also unconstitutional and is quashed and sent back. The challenge to the second ruling only disputed how the courts interpreted the law, so it was not accepted.

who: Losing candidates in local and grassroots elections
Candidates in the elections covered by the rule
Courts handling recount requests
Election commissions

raw.answer: Several people were convicted under Taiwan's Criminal Code Article 146 for moving their household registration to an election district where they did not really live, so they could vote there. The Constitutional Court ruled that the election-fraud rules and the penalty for attempts are constitutional. It also ruled that the Supreme Court judgment against the airline union members was wrong, because it ignored long-term work as a way of really living in a district.
raw.held: Article 146 paragraphs 1, 2 and the attempt provision in paragraph 3 (as applied to paragraph 2) are not unconstitutional, and the petitions challenging them are dismissed. Supreme Court judgment 111 Tai-Shang 1861 is unconstitutional, set aside, and sent back to the Supreme Court; the remaining petitions of petitioners 1 to 5 are not accepted.

points.text: Paragraph 1 is clear enough: 'fraud' has an ordinary meaning, 'other illegal methods' can be understood from that example and from election laws, and a required result and causation further limit it.
Paragraph 2 restricts the right to choose where to vote, but it serves the especially important goal of keeping elections democratically legitimate and fair.
Criminal punishment is the least harmful effective means, since administrative checks cannot fully stop abuse, and the benefit is proportionate to the restriction.
Not punishing people who move registration for other reasons is not unequal treatment, because those reasons are unrelated to the election-fairness goal.
The wording of paragraph 2 uses everyday terms that ordinary people can understand and courts can review.
Punishing attempts is proportionate because most people who falsely move their registration go on to vote, so the danger to the public interest is high.
The lower courts wrongly limited 'actually living' to home life or lodging and ignored the petitioners' decades of work in Taoyuan, so the Supreme Court judgment is set aside and sent back.

who: Voters who move their household registration
People who work long-term in a district away from home
Petitioners convicted of false registration
Courts that apply the rule

raw.answer: Several landowners were taxed land value tax on land that they let the public pass through for free, because the land counted as the legally required open space around a building. They argued that the rule denying an exemption for that land violated the Constitution. The court held that the rule does not violate the equal protection principle, rejected one person's challenge to a court judgment, and declined to hear the remaining claims.
raw.held: The proviso in Article 9 of the Land Tax Reduction and Exemption Rules, which denies the land value tax exemption for legally required open space on building sites, does not violate equal protection in Article 7 of the Constitution. Petitioner four's request to review the court judgment was rejected, and the other requests were not accepted.

points.text: The rule's purpose is legitimate. It aims at fair sharing of the tax burden and at keeping the exemption from becoming too loose.
The tax rules treat differences in tax treatment leniently. If the purpose is proper and the classification is reasonably related to it, equal protection is satisfied.
The wording 'legally required open space' replaced 'required open space' only as a change of terms, with no change in meaning. Its content follows the Building Act and local building rules.

Legally required open space is part of the building site and serves light, ventilation, fire safety and similar functions. Its owner keeps benefits such as counting it toward the required open space and sharing in redevelopment. Purely private road land given to the public gives its owner no such benefit, so taxing the two differently is reasonably related to fair taxation.

Petitioner four's claims about forged documents and the land's classification are only disputes over how facts and law were applied. The Ministry of the Interior's letter treating private access roads within a building site as legally required open space raises no constitutional doubt, so the review request was rejected.

Some claims were not accepted. Petitioner one did not specifically show what was unconstitutional, and petitioner two challenged administrative actions and judgments, which cannot be the object of an interpretation request.

who: Landowners who let the public pass over their land for free
Owners of building sites with legally required open space
Tax authorities assessing land value tax

raw.answer: Two senior staff at a financial holding company were convicted for planning to acquire over 20% of a listed company's shares without using a public tender offer, as the Securities and Exchange Act requires. They asked the Constitutional Court to review the criminal provisions on the grounds that they were too vague and gave regulators too open an authorization. The court found the provisions did not violate the constitution on either ground.
raw.held: The criminal rules punishing failure to use a public tender offer (Securities and Exchange Act Art. 175, Art. 43-1(3) and (4), and Art. 11(1) of the tender offer rules), read together, are consistent with the principle of clear criminal law. The authorization to the regulator in Art. 43-1(4) is also consistent with the principle of clear delegation.

points.text: Although these are economic crime rules, they are still criminal law, so they must meet the constitutional requirements of legality and clarity in criminal punishment.

In judging clarity, the 'ordinary person bound by the rule' means large-share acquirers, who have more market expertise than the average person. Because the rule borrows details from regulator-made rules, the provisions must be read together.
Read together, 'planning to acquire' can be understood as agreeing in advance to acquire, so 'planning to acquire within 50 days' means agreeing within 50 days to acquire.
Setting the threshold at 20% was within the regulator's own authority, and large acquirers could foresee that 'a certain proportion' includes 20% or more.
The regulator's 2005 letter to a third party differed in no real way from the 2007 letter, and it was not published or binding on the petitioners, so the claim of unclear rules failed.

The delegation to the regulator is clear in purpose, content and scope: to set the tender-offer threshold and exemptions, adjusting quickly to market changes. The parent law also lets people foresee that they may be punished.

who: Large-share acquirers and company executives
Persons planning to acquire 20% or more of a listed company
The financial regulator (Financial Supervisory Commission)
Defendants in securities cases

raw.answer: An employer was fined for not topping up its labor retirement reserve account to cover the retirement pay of workers expected to qualify to retire the next year. A court hearing the appeal asked whether the Labor Standards Act rule requiring this one-time top-up is unconstitutional. The Constitutional Court decided the rule is constitutional.
raw.held: Article 56, paragraph 2 of the Labor Standards Act, which requires employers to make up the estimated shortfall in the reserve account in one payment by the end of March of the next year, does not violate the proportionality principle, is not contrary to the constitutional protection of property, and does not raise an equal treatment problem.

points.text: The rule limits employers' property rights because it affects how they manage and use their funds, so it must be a reasonable means to a legitimate public purpose.

Its purpose is legitimate: to make employers prepare early so that workers retiring the next year get full legal retirement pay, since the partial-reserve system and flexible contribution rates could leave the reserve short.
The one-time top-up gives early warning and prevention, because the March deadline falls in the year workers qualify to retire.
The amount required is not too broad: it covers only the gap for workers legally entitled to retire the next year, and the gap depends on how well the employer contributed earlier.

Employers get a transition period of over a year, plus offsetting measures: tax deduction of the top-up, a guaranteed return on the fund, and the option to suspend contributions once the reserve is enough.

The rule does not violate equal treatment, because the installment option for paying retirement pay and the top-up duty cover different obligations with different purposes, so they are not comparable.

who: Employers covered by the Labor Standards Act retirement system
Workers expecting to retire
Small and medium-sized businesses

raw.answer: Fifty-two people challenged Taiwan's rules on when criminal judges must step aside because they took part earlier in the same case. The Constitutional Court held that judges who made a final verdict must step aside when that verdict is reviewed through a retrial or extraordinary appeal, and the law must be amended. It upheld the rules that let judges sit again after a case is sent back for retrial within the same court level.
raw.held: Judges who took part in a final verdict must recuse themselves from retrial and extraordinary appeal proceedings on it, with no limit of one time. Lawmakers have 2 years to write this into the Code of Criminal Procedure. The other challenged rules, which let judges sit again after a remand at the same court level, were held constitutional. One Supreme Court ruling was struck down and sent back, and the other challenges and interim-measure requests were dismissed.

points.text: The right to a fair trial requires a judge to step aside when they have a conflict of interest or would be reviewing their own earlier decision.

The recusal rule for judges who took part in the 'prior instance' covers only lower-court rulings. It does not cover earlier rulings at the same court level, and a retrial or extraordinary appeal is not a prior instance.

A judge in a retrial or extraordinary appeal who took part in the final verdict would be reviewing their own work. That undermines trust and the defendant's extraordinary remedy, so recusal is required each time. Administrative and civil procedure already require recusal in retrials, which makes the criminal gap hard to justify.
Only judges who made the final verdict itself must recuse, not those who sat in earlier stages. Judges who sat in earlier stages need not recuse.
The Supreme Court's rules assigning a case back to the same judge are constitutional. They were set in advance and apply generally, and the judge reviews a lower-court ruling, not their own.

A judge who took part in a ruling that was sent back may sit again at the same level, because the defendant still gets a full new hearing. Prior involvement alone does not prove bias, speeds up trials, and avoids running out of eligible judges.

who: Criminal defendants seeking retrial or extraordinary appeal
Criminal court judges
Defendants in cases sent back for retrial
Legislators and judicial authorities

raw.answer: The case was brought by a person who said land inherited from an ancestor, privately owned under Japanese rule, was registered as state land in Taiwan's post-war land registration, and a Supreme Court precedent let the state refuse to return it because 15 years had passed. The Constitutional Court held that in this situation the state cannot use the civil-law limitation period, and that the part of the precedent saying otherwise is inconsistent with the constitutional protection of property.
raw.held: For land that was privately owned under Japanese rule but was registered as state land because the owner missed the land registration deadline, the civil-law limitation period does not apply when the owner asks the state to cancel the registration. The relevant part of Supreme Court precedent 70 Tai-Shang-Zi No. 311 is inconsistent with Article 15 of the Constitution. The petitioner's remaining requests were not accepted for review.

points.text: Article 15 protects property owners' right to use, benefit from and dispose of their property, and an owner whose registration does not match reality can generally ask the registered holder to cancel it and return the land.
The precedent lets the state raise the 15-year limitation period against such claims, which restricts people's constitutionally protected property.
The limitation period exists to settle unclear legal relations and keep legal order stable, but it must also take the right-holder's interests into account and be used in good faith.
Registering Japanese-era private land as state land during the land registration did not change who owned it, so the people remained the true owners and had to claim the land back from the state.
The state is not a holder of Article 15 property rights, and letting it rely on the limitation period would effectively allow it to take private land without expropriation procedures.
Many people missed the deadlines because of the circumstances of the time, so letting the state rely on the limitation period would be contrary to good faith and has no justification.

who: Owners or heirs of land privately owned under Japanese rule and registered as state land
The state as the registered owner
Judges of courts at all levels
The petitioner in this case

raw.answer: A former conscript soldier was convicted by military courts of robbery (snatching property) together with a civilian, but the ordinary courts later acquitted the civilian of the same act. The Constitutional Court held that the military trial law allowing appeals to a higher ordinary court only on the ground that the judgment violated the law was not unconstitutional. It also held that the soldier must be able to seek a retrial because the two courts reached conflicting findings on the same facts.
raw.held: The rule that allows appeals to the High Court only for violation of law is not found contrary to the constitutional right to sue (Article 16). The petitioner may apply for a retrial of the military judgment at the Taiwan High Court Kaohsiung Branch within 30 days of service of this ruling; the remaining requests were not accepted.

points.text: The right to sue under Article 16 covers soldiers too, and military trials must meet the minimum of due process; fairness is required when a soldier is tried separately from a civilian co-offender.

How appeal levels are designed, including the split between fact-finding and legal review, is mainly for the legislature. The rule's purpose was only to let convicted defendants challenge violations of law in ordinary courts, so omitting appeals on factual error is not unconstitutional. Review of such violations can also go through the Prosecutor General's extraordinary appeal.

The same fact cannot both be a crime and not a crime. If an ordinary court acquits a co-offender on the same main evidence, the soldier's military conviction raises reasonable doubt about its factual accuracy.

Under the presumption of innocence and resolving doubt in the defendant's favor, the convicted soldier must be able to seek a retrial on this ground, and possibly without the usual requirement of new facts or evidence, to avoid wrongful conviction.
Because the law gave no such retrial ground, soldiers' Article 16 right was infringed and the due process requirement was not met. Retrial is to be sought at the corresponding ordinary court.

The challenge to the military trial law's Article 1 was not accepted because the provision was later amended and the dispute no longer exists. The request for a supplementary interpretation was unnecessary because the law had already been amended.

who: Convicted soldiers tried in military courts
Civilian co-defendants tried in ordinary courts
The petitioner, a former conscript
Military and ordinary courts

raw.answer: A civil servant at Taiwan's National Property Administration slipped on a step while on an assigned site visit and broke a foot bone. His request for a 10,000 NT dollar injury condolence payment was refused because the accident was his own carelessness and not a sudden outside danger. The Constitutional Court held that the statute itself is constitutional and its word 'accident' includes the worker's own carelessness, but that the rule limiting accidents to 'outside danger' events goes beyond the statute and violates the constitutional right to hold public office.
raw.held: Article 21(2), first part, of the Civil Servants Protection Act is not unconstitutional, and 'accident' in it includes accidents caused by the civil servant's own carelessness. The words 'outside danger event' in Article 3(1) of the 2018 payment rules add a limit the law does not have and violate Article 18 of the Constitution. The petitioner's other challenges were not accepted for review.

points.text: The right to hold public office in Article 18 covers job-safety protection, including proper care for civil servants injured or made ill in the course of duty.
The payment, though called 'condolence money', is a statutory benefit and a form of work-injury compensation, so the implementing rules must fit the parent law.

The statute's 'accident' is a state guarantee that gives concrete effect to the right to hold public office, so it is not limited to outside dangers and includes the civil servant's own carelessness. The statute is therefore not unconstitutional.

The rules' definition requires an 'outside danger' and so excludes accidents caused by the civil servant's own carelessness. That adds a limit the parent law lacks and does not fit the occupational safety law's purpose, so it violates the constitutional protection.

The Ministry of Examination's reply said agencies had asked for the 'accident' requirement to be loosened. Proof of sudden outside forces is hard, and personal fault is hard to separate from other causes. The rules were amended in 2021 to drop the 'danger' element.
The petitioner's challenges to other provisions were not accepted because he did not explain how they objectively conflict with the Constitution.

who: Civil servants injured, disabled or killed in the course of duty
Families of civil servants who die on duty
Government agencies that decide condolence payment claims
The petitioner, whose retrial the ruling allows

raw.answer: A law firm's Hsinchu branch was searched and its client emails seized in an insider-trading investigation of a client company. The firm argued that the search and seizure rules violate the Constitution. The court held that the rules are partly unconstitutional because they do not exclude confidential lawyer-client defense communications and the documents made from them, but that having no special search procedure for law offices is acceptable.
raw.held: The search and seizure rules must be amended within 2 years to exclude confidential communications between lawyers and defendants, suspects or potential suspects, and the documents arising from them. Until then judges, prosecutors and officials must follow the ruling. The lack of a special procedure for searching law offices does not violate the Constitution, and the remaining requests were not accepted.

points.text: Free, private communication between a defense lawyer and a defendant is protected by the right to bring a lawsuit and to defend oneself. It also covers suspects and people who may become suspects.

That protection extends to the documents and electronic records a lawyer makes through such communication, which are the core of the lawyer-client relationship. Letting the state search or seize them blocks the lawyer's role and wrongly harms the lawyer's right to work.

The current rules do not exclude these materials from search and seizure, so to that extent they conflict with the Constitution. This does not apply where there is evidence the lawyer destroyed or forged evidence or colluded with co-offenders or witnesses.
Law offices hold the secrets of many clients, and searching them inevitably exposes other clients' protected materials. That calls for special care in conditions, procedure and remedies.

Existing law already requires a judge to authorize searches and to scrutinize strictly any application to search a law office. The warrant must define the scope and exclude protected communications, and officials should first order documents handed over.

Existing law also provides safeguards during and after the search, including recording, sealing disputed items for court review, reporting results to the court, and challenging the search. Wrongly seized items are returned, and evidence from a revoked seizure can be barred. So no special law-office procedure is required.

who: Lawyers and law firms
Defendants and criminal suspects
Potential suspects who seek legal advice
Judges, prosecutors and investigators

raw.answer: Eight petitioners, including judges hearing drug cases and people already sentenced, argued that the law setting death or life imprisonment as the only penalties for selling Class 1 drugs is unconstitutional. The Constitutional Court held that, for very minor cases, the rule is too harsh even after a judge reduces the sentence under Criminal Code Article 59, so it violates the Constitution. It gave lawmakers two years to fix the law and allowed courts to reduce sentences further in the meantime.
raw.held: The fixed minimum of life imprisonment for selling Class 1 drugs is unconstitutional for cases with no other crimes and extremely minor, forgivable circumstances; the relevant authorities must amend it within 2 years, and until then courts may cut the sentence by up to half beyond the Article 59 reduction. Part of petitioner 8's request was not accepted.

points.text: The Constitution protects personal liberty, and a prison sentence must match the harm caused and the offender's blame; a punishment beyond that is unconstitutional.
The law's purpose is serious: Class 1 drugs are the most addictive and harmful, and selling drugs feeds the supply of harm, so lawmakers chose heavy punishment to protect public health and order.
Even so, Class 1 drug selling covers a huge range, from large smuggling groups to small sales between users or merely handing over drugs, yet the law gives one fixed minimum of life imprisonment.

Courts usually apply Article 59 and sentence within 15 to 20 years, but for extremely minor, forgivable cases with no other crimes this is still too harsh and out of proportion to blame, so the rule violates the proportionality principle.
As a temporary measure until the law is amended, courts may reduce the sentence by up to half in such cases, and petitioners 4 to 8 may ask the Prosecutor General to file an extraordinary appeal.

The court also suggested lawmakers consider adding fixed-term prison sentences or setting penalties by quantity or number of sales, noting that possession and transfer of Class 1 drugs already vary by quantity.

who: People convicted of selling Class 1 drugs in very minor cases
Judges hearing such cases
Petitioners 4 to 8
Legislators and authorities who must amend the law

raw.answer: Three people were convicted of selling drugs after earlier naming their drug supplier. The supplier was caught only after their convictions became final. They asked for a retrial under Code of Criminal Procedure Article 420(1)(6), which allows a retrial when new evidence shows the person should have received an exemption from punishment. Courts rejected them because the law they relied on says punishment is to be reduced or waived, not simply waived. The Constitutional Court ruled that the retrial rule must cover laws that say punishment is 'reduced or waived' as well as laws that say it is 'waived'.
raw.held: The phrase 'should receive... exemption from punishment' in Article 420(1)(6) must cover laws providing for 'reduced or waived' punishment as well as laws providing for 'waived' punishment, or it violates the equal protection guaranteed by Article 7 of the Constitution. The petitioners may apply for a retrial in their own cases within 30 days of the judgment being delivered to them.

points.text: Under the wording, 'should receive exemption from punishment' means exemption the law requires. Laws saying 'reduced or waived' mean a court could objectively be required to waive punishment, as can laws saying 'waived'.

The purpose of retrial is to find the truth and achieve justice, not to favor legal finality. Acquittal, dismissal and exemption from punishment are grouped together because each permanently bars the state from punishing, so justice outweighs finality. This also holds where a court could waive punishment under a 'reduced or waived' law.

The 2015 amendment removed the word 'certain' from 'certain new evidence' to lower the threshold for a retrial and avoid wrongful imprisonment. People under 'reduced or waived' laws have the same need for effective relief.

The retrial-opening stage only asks whether new evidence raises reasonable doubt and could lead to exemption from punishment. It does not decide whether exemption will actually be given, so people under 'reduced or waived' laws should also be able to reach a retrial.
Because laws of both kinds let courts objectively order exemption, they are alike and must be treated alike under the equal protection guarantee of Article 7, absent a justification.

who: People convicted whose law provides 'reduced or waived' punishment
The three petitioners in drug cases
Courts hearing retrial requests

raw.answer: A company wholly owned by overseas shareholders was ordered to pay back the excess tax credits it had wrongly recorded as given to its shareholders. It challenged the income tax rule behind that order. The court held that the rule violates the constitutional right to equality when applied to companies whose shareholders are all non-residents or overseas businesses without a fixed place of business or agent in Taiwan.
raw.held: The rule is unconstitutional, and from the date of the judgment's announcement it no longer has effect, but only as applied to companies whose shareholders are all non-resident individuals or overseas businesses with no fixed place of business or business agent in Taiwan. The exception is the credit arising from the 10% surtax actually paid on undistributed earnings.

points.text: Requiring companies to keep a shareholder imputation credit account and accurate records is a permissible duty that serves the public interest.
Overseas shareholders are taxed by withholding at source and generally cannot use the imputation credit, so an erroneous account entry normally costs the state no tax.

The one exception is the credit from the 10% surtax on undistributed earnings, which overseas shareholders may use and which can be calculated separately, so errors there could cost the state revenue.
For companies with domestic shareholders, making the company pay back the excess has a proper purpose and a reasonable link to preventing revenue loss and keeping tax collection efficient.

For companies whose shareholders are all overseas, the rule requires repayment regardless of any possible revenue loss. This sweeps too broadly and treats different situations the same without reasonable basis, which violates equality under Article 7.

who: Companies whose shareholders are all overseas
Non-resident individual shareholders
Overseas businesses without a fixed place or agent in Taiwan
Companies with domestic shareholders

raw.answer: Two people asked to be recognized as members (paxia yuan) of ancestral worship associations, but the associations' other members did not list them and the courts rejected their claims. The Constitutional Court held that the rules limiting membership to male-line descendants, and only to certain daughters, violate the constitutional guarantee of gender equality. It also set out how the excluded female-line descendants can ask to be listed.
raw.held: Article 4, paragraph 1 (latter part) and paragraph 2 of the Ancestral Worship Association Act are unconstitutional because they leave out the founder's other female-line descendants. Those descendants not yet listed can submit proof that they are the founder's direct descendants and ask to be listed, with rights and duties from the day they ask, without affecting rights and obligations already carried out by existing members. The remaining parts of the petitions were not accepted.

points.text: Because the rules sort people by sex, which is hard to change and tied to historical stereotypes, the court applied intermediate scrutiny: the aim must be an important public interest and the classification must be substantially related to it.
The legislature's stated aims were respecting traditional ancestor-succession custom and the rule against retroactive law.

The non-retroactivity aim does not hold: the old custom was not a legal rule, no law set membership before the Act, and the Act applies to relationships continuing after it took effect, so it is not retroactive application.

The main purpose of these associations is worshipping ancestors and honoring filial duty. Male-line and female-line descendants do not differ in carrying on worship, nor in willingness or ability to take part, so continuing the distinction is outdated and may even harm that purpose.

Under Article 7 and Additional Article 10, paragraph 6 of the Constitution, the state must work to remove gender discrimination and should not legislate to endorse discriminatory customs, so the aim is not an important public interest and the means are not proper.
The rules treat people differently by sex, and paragraph 2 also by marriage or by taking the mother's surname, so they conflict with gender equality under Article 7.

who: Female-line descendants of association founders not yet listed as members
Existing members of ancestral worship associations
Ancestral worship associations without rules on membership
The two petitioners

raw.answer: The case was about a provision of Taiwan's Civil Code (Article 1052, paragraph 2, proviso) that bars a spouse who is solely at fault for a marriage's breakdown from asking a court for divorce. The Constitutional Court held that the bar is generally consistent with the constitutional protection of freedom of marriage. It is unconstitutional, though, where it flatly denies divorce regardless of how long ago the breakdown happened or how long it has lasted, and so is clearly too harsh in a particular case.
raw.held: The at-fault-spouse restriction is generally constitutional, but to the extent it absolutely denies the solely at-fault spouse any chance of divorce regardless of elapsed time, and is clearly too harsh in an individual case, it violates freedom of marriage. The relevant authorities must amend it within 2 years of the judgment; if they do not, courts must decide such cases according to this judgment.

points.text: Freedom of marriage under Article 22 includes the freedom to end a marriage, including asking a court for divorce when the spouses cannot agree, so the restriction is an interference that must be justified.

The restriction's purpose is legitimate: it strengthens the blameless spouse's right to decide whether to keep or end the marriage, prevents arbitrary divorce requests, and protects the marriage legal order and public sense of right, including children's interests.

Under Taiwan's multiple-ground divorce system the restriction is not wholly unhelpful to that purpose, and it generally prioritizes the blameless spouse's freedom to maintain the marriage, so in principle it is not contrary to freedom of marriage.

Marriages usually break down from many causes built up over time. Where the marriage is beyond repair, forbidding the solely at-fault spouse from ever seeking divorce preserves only an outward shell and may harm children.

Because the rule applies regardless of how long the breakdown has lasted, it completely deprives the at-fault spouse of any chance to divorce and can be clearly too harsh in individual cases. The two spouses' freedoms must be balanced, so the rule fails in that range.

How long the period must be is left to the legislature. The court also suggested reforms such as a separation system, a hardship clause, and protections for the blameless or weaker spouse and children.

who: Spouses solely at fault for a marriage breakdown
Blameless spouses who want to keep the marriage
Children of couples in divorce cases
Courts and lawmakers

raw.answer: A judge hearing a medical-law case asked the Constitutional Court whether Article 84 of the Medical Care Act, which says only medical institutions may run medical advertising, is constitutional as applied to doctors. The court decided that banning doctors from medical advertising violates the constitutional protection of free speech. That part of the rule stops having effect from the day the judgment is announced.
raw.held: The part of Article 84 that bans doctors from medical advertising conflicts with the free speech guarantee in Article 11 of the Constitution, and it loses effect from the date of the judgment's announcement.

points.text: Medical advertising is also a form of speech: it shows the doctor's expertise and gives the public information for choosing care, so even doctors keep free speech rights about their profession.
The court applied a mid-level test: since protecting public health is an important public interest, the state may restrict such speech only by means that have a substantial connection to that goal.

The rule's purposes were easier administration and protecting public health. Administrative convenience alone is not an important public interest, but protecting public health is, so the purpose itself did not violate the Constitution.

A total ban on doctors advertising has no substantial connection to protecting health: doctors' information helps patients choose, and no evidence was offered that allowing it would lead to improper ads, although doctors were allowed to advertise for over 40 years before 1986.

A doctor's ability to advertise is a separate matter from whether a medical institution may advertise, and a doctor's own advertising cannot be replaced by the institution's, so it deserves independent free speech protection.
The ban therefore fails the proportionality principle in Article 23 and conflicts with the free speech guarantee in Article 11.

who: Doctors
Patients and the public
Medical institutions
Health authorities

raw.answer: Several judges asked Taiwan's Constitutional Court to review a law that removes years worked for the Kuomintang and certain affiliated groups from public servants' pension calculations and requires repayment of the resulting overpayments. The court held that the law's key provisions do not violate the Constitution, and it declined to hear the remaining parts of the petitions.
raw.held: The court held that the listed provisions of the law (the group list, the recalculation and repayment rules, the repayment duty of the groups, and the exclusion of limitation periods) are not unconstitutional, and it dismissed the remaining petitions as inadmissible.

points.text: The law names specific groups, but it serves the especially important aim of transitional justice. The groups were chosen because the Examination Yuan had approved counting their service years, so the choice is substantially related to that aim. Counting the Chinese Youth Corps with the other groups does not breach equality.

Recalculating pensions and requiring former political appointees to repay overpayments is retroactive. That is not forbidden when it serves a major public interest. The old orders that counted group service had serious defects and lacked any statutory basis, so recipients had no trust worth protecting.

The pension cuts mainly affect benefits paid from the state budget rather than from the recipients' own contributions, so the legislature has wider room to adjust them. The measures are reasonably connected to restoring the pension system, and there are protections such as a minimum monthly amount and installment payment.

The groups must repay even though they did not receive the money themselves. As employers they should have paid retirement pay to their staff, but the unlawful counting shifted that cost to the state, and they also gained talent-exchange benefits. This gives a reasonable connection, so it is not an improper linkage.

The groups' repayment duty is genuinely retroactive, but it is allowed because of the especially important public interest. The groups helped create the unlawful system and have no protected trust. They are not required to pay interest, so the burden is not excessive.

Excluding the usual limitation periods does not breach legal certainty. Transitional justice legislation only became possible after the Kuomintang lost its legislative majority in 2016, and without the exclusion it would be hard to carry out.

who: Retired public servants whose group service years were counted
Former political appointees ordered to repay
The Kuomintang and affiliated groups such as the Chinese Youth Corps
Agencies that grant pensions
